articles.title: AI’s Intrusion into Public Education
articles.author: Jake Colosa, Ann Finkel, Katie Punsly and Erin Tabor
articles.content_excerpt: Think back to the first day of school when you were a kid. You walked into the building feeling nervous and excited to be reunited with friends, meet your teachers, and crack open your brand new supplies. Now imagine that instead of doing get-to-know-you activities with your classmates, you spend the majority of your day answering questions on a computer, and instead of your teacher picking out a book that she knows will spark your curiosity, you read AI-generated text on a screen. As students and teachers head back to school this fall, this is the bleak reality in more and more classrooms. Unless we fight back, the problem will only get worse. articles.title: How a Canadian Union Finally Bested Walmart
articles.author: Benjamin Y. Fong
articles.content_excerpt: In our hyperpolitical age , when mass protests come and go without much clear sense of what was won or lost, the strategies of social movements can seem quixotic, their benchmarks of success fuzzy. In the union world, however, success or failure can be measured in more cut-and-dried terms: by the ratification of a union contract. A contract between a union and an employer does not simply lay out the terms of employment at a particular worksite. It is also a symbol of the begrudging respect that an employer has for the collective organization of its employees. Until this year, Walmart had not put pen to paper on a union contract in Canada or the United States. articles.title: Socialize All Housing
articles.author: Mike Beggs
articles.content_excerpt: In 1872, the German socialist newspaper Der Volksstaat ran a series of articles on housing. The breakneck growth of industrial cities had brought overcrowding, squalor, and soaring rents for workers. Their author, Arthur Mülberger, drawing on the ideas of the French anarchist Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, offered a simple solution — tenants should become owners. In the scheme, rental payments would be transformed into something like a mortgage payment. Eventually, every worker would hold the title to their own home. Friedrich Engels was unimpressed. In a series of replies later collected as The Housing Question , the cofounder of Marxism dismissed Mülberger’s plan as both impractical and political malpractice. articles.author: Chip Gibbons
articles.content_excerpt: On Tuesday, September 22, the Spanish Council of Ministers refused to block a US extradition request for James “Fergie” Chambers, a prominent and wealthy leftist activist and donor. The council did not determine whether the US citizen and activist will be sent to the United States, but only whether the request would proceed in Spanish courts, who will then make the final determination. Chambers’s legal team, which includes a number of legendary human rights lawyers, have vowed they will argue before the courts that Chambers’s extradition is politically motivated; thus granting it would violate the US-Spanish extradition treaty. articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content_excerpt: Susan Collins has been the senator from Maine for twenty-nine years, during which time she’s received scrutiny for her coziness with corporate donors , her record on war with Iran , and her votes against lowering prescription drug prices, among other things. But one of the most impactful measures on Maine workers that she took happened well before she first went to Washington. In an episode that’s little remembered today, in the late 1980s and early ’90s, Collins led the way on a set of reforms to Maine’s workers’ compensation system that saw the state government shut down for the first time in its history and led to major cuts to injured workers’ benefits. articles.title: Israel Fears NAZA. Why Don’t Our Films Scare Anyone?
articles.author: Alex McCarron
articles.content_excerpt: It isn’t uncommon for states to retaliate against the filmmakers who insult them. Sergei Parajanov was imprisoned for daring to make poetic cinema in the era of Soviet Realism. Jafar Panahi’s twenty-year ban from filmmaking and six-year prison sentence have become the central theme of the very films the Iranian state seeks to suppress. Even in America, documentarians like Emile de Antonio, Errol Morris, and Frederick Wiseman have faced bans, bomb threats, and personal death threats. Within the long history of the repression of film and filmmakers, it’s hard to think of anything like the fury the Israeli state is raining down on the directors of NAZA , a new documentary tracing the IDF’s brutal campaign in Gaza.
